review_notes: I read the whole file and searched the formal-frontier root for uses of `evalSectionToEventualRange`. It is used only in its own surjectivity statement and in a test client. Nothing in the file is a simp lemma and nothing is tagged `@[simp]`. The proofs use `simpa only` and `rw` with explicit lemma lists, so I found no competing rules or loops. I did not run Lean. The only simp-interface gap I found is the missing value lemma for the new def.

findings.excerpt: fun x ↦ ⟨x.val i, F.mem_eventualRange_iff.2 fun _ g ↦ ⟨x.val _, x.property g⟩⟩
findings.problem: This is a new public def whose value is a subtype element built by an anonymous constructor. It comes with no simp lemma giving its coercion, `(F.evalSectionToEventualRange i x : F.obj i) = x.val i`. The def is not reducible and is not marked `@[simps]`. Anyone who needs to compute with it, for example to show that the surjectivity statement really gives a section with a prescribed value, must unfold the definition by hand or use `show`/`change`. The file's own proof of `surjective_evalSectionToEventualRange` ends with a `change (y.val i).val = x.val` step instead of a simp-normal rewrite, which suggests the missing lemma.
findings.proposed_change: Add a coercion lemma right after the def, for example `@[simp] theorem coe_evalSectionToEventualRange (F : Jᵒᵖ ⥤ Type w) (i : Jᵒᵖ) (x : F.sections) : (F.evalSectionToEventualRange i x : F.obj i) = x.val i := rfl`. Alternatively, put `@[simps]` on a version that has an explicit structure. The orientation is safe, because the right-hand side is a plain function application with no `evalSectionToEventualRange` on it.
findings.benefit: `simp` can then reduce goals that mention the evaluation map to `x.val i`. Users of the exported API and the surjectivity theorem need not unfold the def. This would also allow `Subtype.ext_iff` style goals to be closed by `simp`.
